title: The Day the Mona Lisa Vanished
description: How a 1911 theft turned a quiet Renaissance portrait into the most famous painting on Earth

concepts.title: A Portrait Before It Was an Icon
concepts.contentHtml:
Start with the most famous painting in the world, and a surprise: for most of its life it was not. The Mona Lisa is Leonardo da Vinci's portrait of Lisa Gherardini, the wife of a rich Florentine silk merchant, Francesco del Giocondo. Leonardo began it around 1503 and kept working on it for years; the Louvre dates it 1503 to 1519. It is painted in oil on a thin panel of poplar wood, about 79 by 53 centimetres, big enough to show the sitter at life size. You can see it today in the Louvre in Paris.

Picture it as the Louvre's curators describe it. Lisa sits on a chair with a rounded back, her body turned three-quarters towards you, her right hand resting on her left on the arm of the chair. Behind her, two small columns at the ends of a balustrade frame a vast landscape of mountains and rivers, with a winding road on the left and a bridge on the right. Leonardo built her face from imperceptible transitions between light and shadow, laid on in thin, oily glazes; this soft blurring of edges is called sfumato. Here is a "wait, really?" detail: the picture now wears many thick layers of later varnish, which have yellowed into a filter that turns the blue sky green.1

Its travels began early. Leonardo took the panel with him when he moved to France in 1516, King Francis I bought it, and after the French Revolution it went to the Louvre (Napoleon took it away to hang in his bedroom for a while). Copies were made from the sixteenth century onwards, and more than a hundred are known. Yet outside a small circle of experts it was no household name. Critics only began to hail it as a masterwork in the 1860s, and in 1911 it was not even the most famous painting in its own gallery.2 What changed everything was a crime.

concepts.title: Monday, 21 August 1911
concepts.contentHtml:
On the morning of Monday, 21 August 1911, while the Louvre was still closed to visitors, the Mona Lisa left the building. The thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, an Italian handyman who had worked at the museum installing protective glass cases, including the very case around the Mona Lisa. Accounts of exactly how he did it differ, which is normal for a crime reconstructed from later testimony:

  • In one version, Peruggia came in wearing the white smock that all Louvre employees wore, hid until the gallery closed, took the painting out of its frame, and when the gallery reopened walked out with it under his smock.
  • In another, told by the historians James Zug and Dorothy and Tom Hoobler, three Italian handymen (Peruggia and the brothers Vincenzo and Michele Lancelotti) spent the night in an art-supply cupboard, lifted about 200 pounds of painting, frame and glass case off the wall, stripped the panel out and caught a 7:47 express train.

The strangest part came next. For 28 hours nobody noticed the four bare hooks.1 The Louvre was photographing its collection, and works were carried up to the roof because the cameras of the day did not work well indoors, so an empty space looked routine. Finally a still-life painter who had set up his easel in the gallery persuaded a guard to ask the photographers when they would bring it back. They did not have it.

Then came the frenzy. Newspapers worldwide ran the story, and the New York Times reported 60 detectives on the case. Suspicion fell on the American banker J. P. Morgan, on the German Kaiser and on the avant-garde. The poet Guillaume Apollinaire was arrested and questioned for a week, and Pablo Picasso was questioned too; there was no evidence against either.2 After a week's closure the Louvre reopened to mobs of visitors, the writer Franz Kafka among them, who came to stare at the empty spot that had become a "mark of shame" for Parisians.

concepts.title: Florence, 1913: How a Theft Made a Star
concepts.contentHtml:
Peruggia had stolen something he could not sell. Within days newspapers were offering rewards, and the painting became, as James Zug puts it, too hot to hock. So Peruggia hid it in the false bottom of a trunk in his Paris lodgings and waited. More than two years later, in November 1913, calling himself "Leonardo Vincenzo", he wrote to a Florence art dealer, Alfredo Geri, offering to bring the painting to Italy for a reward of 500,000 lire.1

The next month he carried it to Florence by train in the same trunk and took it to Geri's gallery. Geri called in the head of an Italian art gallery to look, and a stamp on the back confirmed it was the real thing. Peruggia was persuaded to leave it for examination, and the police arrested him later that day. (His hotel shrewdly renamed itself the Hotel La Gioconda.) Peruggia said he was a patriot returning a painting that Napoleon had stolen from Italy. He was wrong: Leonardo had taken it to France himself, and the French king had bought it. Many Italians cheered anyway, crowds flocked to see it at the Uffizi Gallery, and by one account he was sentenced to just eight months in prison before the painting went home to Paris.

The Louvre itself now says plainly what the theft did: it gave the painting worldwide, and above all popular, fame.2 After its rediscovery in 1913 the Mona Lisa became the Louvre's chief masterpiece and the most famous artwork in the world, endlessly reused by artists and advertisers alike. Keep two ideas from this story for the rest of the topic. First, the value of an artwork rests partly on the story attached to it, which is exactly what forgers exploit. Second, a famous stolen painting is almost impossible to sell, which is why art thieves so often end up stuck with their loot.

title: Empty Frames: The Gardner Heist
description: The biggest art theft in history, what was taken, and why thieves steal art they cannot sell

concepts.title: 81 Minutes in Boston
concepts.contentHtml:
The largest art heist in history took place in a museum designed never to change. Isabella Stewart Gardner turned her Italian-inspired palace in Boston and her art collection into a public museum in 1903. She created it so that her collection would be on permanent display "for the education and enjoyment of the public forever", and her will says nothing in it may change. As the museum's conservators put it, they add nothing, sell nothing and rearrange nothing.

In the early hours of 18 March 1990, after Boston's St Patrick's Day celebrations, two men dressed as Boston police officers buzzed the side entrance on the intercom and told the night guard they were investigating a disturbance. He let them in. The thieves handcuffed him and a co-worker and left them in the basement.1 Then, over 81 minutes, they took 13 works of art now worth at least half a billion dollars.2

What happened next is a story of absences. No one has been arrested. None of the 13 works has been recovered. The museum offers a reward of $10 million for information leading to their return, and works with the FBI, which in 2013 announced that it knew who had orchestrated the heist but did not release the names. Anthony Amore, the museum's director of security, is clear about the priority: "Our goal is just recovery, not prosecution or 'whodunnit?'" Decades later the case is still open, and it has become the great cold case of the art world.

concepts.title: What Was Taken, and the Frames Left Behind
concepts.contentHtml:
Most of the stolen works hung in a single gallery, the Dutch Room. The greatest loss was Vermeer's The Concert (1663–1666), one of only about 34 to 36 paintings by him known to exist (counts differ). It is a canvas about two feet square showing three people making music. A man playing the lute sits with his back to you, on a chair whose back is an extraordinary red; to his left a woman sits with her hands poised over the keys of a harpsichord; to the right another stands on the verge of breaking into song.

In the same room hung Rembrandt's Christ in the Storm on the Sea of Galilee, the only seascape he is known to have painted,1 and his A Lady and Gentleman in Black. In all the thieves took three Rembrandts, five drawings by Degas, and works by Flinck and Manet, among others.

Then came a decision that made the gallery famous. Anne Hawley had just been hired as the museum's director when the thieves struck. Afterwards she felt that the empty frames left behind should go back on the wall,2 "so that it would remind visitors, and ourselves, of what we had lost and be a sign of mourning for all of us." They still hang there, and because Gardner's will forbids changes, nothing may take the missing pictures' place. One report called the room a crime scene purposely stuck in time. In 2025, during a floor-to-ceiling restoration of the Dutch Room, conservators restored the empty frames too, ready for the paintings' return. The frames are now a sight in their own right, though Amore thinks the crowds they draw would be dwarfed by the numbers who would come to see "a Vermeer or Rembrandt's only seascape."

concepts.title: Why Steal What You Cannot Sell?
concepts.contentHtml:
Films have taught us to imagine a reclusive billionaire who orders a heist so he can admire a stolen Vermeer in a secret vault. Investigators see little sign of such people. "People don't buy masterpieces to hide them," says Anthony Amore. "And people don't buy stolen art to hide it.1" The real problem for art thieves is the one Peruggia met in 1911: a famous stolen work is instantly recognisable, so no honest buyer will touch it. A Connecticut mobster, Robert Gentile, long suspected of handling some of the Gardner works, reportedly told an informant: "Worth nothing. It's worthless. Nobody wants it."

So what is stolen art good for? Often it becomes a bargaining chip with the authorities. The writer Ulrich Boser, who named a Boston mobster, David Turner, and his friend George Reissfelder as the likely thieves, argued in 2013 that if Turner knew where the paintings were he would use them as a "get-out-of-jail-free card". A retired FBI agent believes a mob crew from Dorchester did the job and that informants tracked the art to Connecticut and Philadelphia; Gentile once told an undercover agent he could sell two of the paintings for $500,000 each, but denied everything until his death in 2021. Searches have found nothing, so treat every theory as unproven.

History still gives grounds for hope. Recoveries, that agent says, tend to come right after a theft or a generation later, when a family clears out an attic or a safe deposit box, and Amore notes that the last time a Rembrandt was stolen and destroyed was almost a hundred years ago. Some cases never close, though. In April 1934 a panel of the Ghent Altarpiece, The Righteous Judges, was stolen from St Bavo's Cathedral in Ghent. The thief sent twelve ransom notes, and a stockbroker, Arsène Goedertier, made a deathbed confession without revealing where it was. It has never been seen since: the panel on view today is a copy painted in 1945 by Jef Van der Veken, an artist and occasional forger.2

title: The Forger Who Swindled Göring
description: Han van Meegeren's fake Vermeers: how he made them, who fell for them and how he was caught

concepts.title: A Gap in Vermeer
concepts.contentHtml:
To forge a great artist, it helps to pick one with gaps. Johannes Vermeer of Delft (1632–1675) left only about 35 or 36 paintings,1 where a contemporary such as Rembrandt typically produced ten times as many, and his biography is almost a complete blank. After 1866, when the French critic Théophile Thoré brought much of Vermeer's misidentified work together, his reputation soared, and collectors and scholars began hunting for more. The critic James Fenton calls the result "Vermeermania".

Han van Meegeren was a Dutch painter of limited ability with a grudge against modern art, which he attacked in his own magazine in the language of Nazi cultural propaganda. His key insight was psychological. An imitation that comes very close to a famous artist makes experts hunt for the last small difference. So instead of copying Vermeer's familiar interiors, he painted something nobody had seen: a large religious scene with only hints of Vermeer, and let the experts fill in the gap themselves. Rather than asking why it looked like no known Vermeer, they decided Vermeer had been an even greater genius than anyone knew.

The result was The Supper at Emmaus (1937), an oil on canvas 118 by 130.5 centimetres, faintly signed "IVmeer" in the upper left. It shows the Gospel story in which the risen Christ reveals himself to his disciples, and it is larger than anything Vermeer was known to have painted. On the recommendation of the great scholar Abraham Bredius, the Museum Boijmans Van Beuningen in Rotterdam bought it as an extraordinary Vermeer, right under the nose of the Rijksmuseum.2 Look closely and you can spot a borrowing: a hand and forearm are a botched copy from Vermeer's The Astronomer. The museum still owns it, now identified as a fake, and says it is one of the audience's favourites.

concepts.title: Plastic, an Oven and Real Ultramarine
concepts.contentHtml:
A new oil painting is soft: oil paint takes decades to harden fully, and pressing a finger into a recent blob of paint can leave a dent. A three-hundred-year-old Vermeer had to be hard as stone. Van Meegeren bought an oven and tried time and again to mix paints that would survive baking, but they burned or melted, until he hit on dissolving a small amount of plastic into the paint. Baked, it hardened without losing its brilliance.

Everything else was chosen to survive inspection:

  • Old canvases. He scraped the paint off genuine seventeenth-century pictures by obscure artists and reused the canvases, so the support itself really was old.
  • Period pigments. Early in 1931 he bought natural ultramarine, made from ground lapis lazuli and then more expensive than gold by weight, from the London firm Winsor & Newton. A Scotland Yard file released in 2010 suggests he may have bought the equivalent of eight years of the firm's sales.1
  • Momentum. Once Emmaus was accepted, each new "Vermeer" only had to resemble the Vermeer he had invented, not the real one, so his task got easier with every sale.

His biblical series sold for fortunes: by one estimate he pocketed the equivalent of $30 million. The most notorious buyer was Hermann Göring, the second most powerful man in Nazi Germany, who traded 137 looted paintings for2 Christ with the Woman Taken in Adultery (1942). That picture hid a slip. With the war on, van Meegeren could no longer buy natural ultramarine, so he used a modern cobalt blue instead.3 The scientific examination made for his trial found natural ultramarine in Christ's robe in Emmaus, and the modern blue in the picture sold to Göring.

concepts.title: Traitor or Hero?
concepts.contentHtml:
The Göring sale was van Meegeren's undoing. The Nazis kept meticulous records, and after the war the paperwork for Göring's prize "Vermeer" led police to his door in Amsterdam in 1945. Selling a national treasure to the enemy looked like collaboration, a far graver charge than fraud. So van Meegeren made an astonishing confession: the "Vermeer" was no national treasure at all, because he had painted it himself, along with Emmaus.

To prove it, he offered to paint a new "Vermeer" of his own composition. He was supplied with a seventeenth-century canvas, special brushes and rare paints, and worked in the presence of several witnesses1 on a scene of the young Christ teaching in the Temple among the scribes. A press photograph from October 1945, now in the Rijksmuseum, shows him putting the finishing touches to it in his studio in Amsterdam. That busts a popular myth: he did not paint a fake in the courtroom. The demonstration happened in his studio, long before his trial in 1947.

In 1947 he was convicted and sentenced to a year in prison,2 but he died of a heart attack a month or two later (sources differ) without serving a day. By then he was a folk hero. He styled himself a patriot who had swindled the Nazi leader, and the Dutch public loved it. Historians are less charmed. He had mixed with the Nazis during the occupation, and James Fenton describes him as a fascist and an antisemite whose wartime fakes carry a fascist fantasy of Dutch national identity and "look nothing like Vermeer3". His victims paid too: Dirk Hannema, the Boijmans director who bought Emmaus, was later branded a collaborator and spent decades in disgrace. The question worth asking is why experts once thought the fakes looked like Vermeer at all.

title: Forgers Against the Art World
description: Michelangelo's fake antique, Hebborn's drawings, Keating's Sexton Blakes and Beltracchi's lost masterpieces

concepts.title: Revenge Served at Auction: Eric Hebborn
concepts.contentHtml:
Forgery is far older than the modern art market. In 1496 the 21-year-old Michelangelo carved a marble Sleeping Eros (a sleeping Cupid), kept it buried in the earth for a time so that it picked up stains and marks,1 and sold it through a middleman to Cardinal Raffaele Riario, a great collector of Roman antiquities, as an ancient statue. The joke turned twice. When the cardinal grew suspicious and returned it, Michelangelo had become the most famous sculptor in Rome, so the dealer happily resold it as an original Michelangelo. The statue is now lost.

Many later forgers share a motive that the art historian Noah Charney sums up as revenge on the art world. Eric Hebborn, an artist whose own work never succeeded, once sold some drawings he had found at a flea market to the London dealers Colnaghi and doubled his money. Weeks later he saw the same drawings in their window, priced in the thousands of pounds. Feeling cheated, he decided to get back at them.

His method was cunning. For most of history, drawings were working sketches for paintings and nobody collected them, so many are lost. Hebborn chose famous paintings and drew the "preparatory sketches" that might once have existed: a fake that arrives with its own explanation. He used blank pages cut from antique books so the paper would test as old, mixed his own inks and reproduced period pens and brushes.2 Real oak gall ink slowly eats grooves into paper, so for a drawing meant to look 500 years old he advised tracing the lines with sulphuric acid. He made at least a thousand forgeries,3 and Charney thinks some still hang in galleries unrecognised. Hebborn later published his recipes in The Art Forger's Handbook, which has since turned up in the studios of many arrested forgers.

concepts.title: Tom Keating's Sexton Blakes
concepts.contentHtml:
Tom Keating grew up poor in south-east London, the son of a house painter, and won a scholarship to Goldsmiths College, but finished in 1952 without the diploma he wanted. He earned a living restoring pictures for small dealers, found he could re-create paintings with ease, and began turning out imitations he called "Sexton Blakes", rhyming slang for fakes. He claimed some two thousand in twenty-five years, from the Canadian painter Cornelius Krieghoff to the English Romantic Samuel Palmer, often on old canvases and paper from friends in the antiques trade, sometimes in modern acrylics or even household emulsion.

In 1976 Geraldine Norman, the art critic of The Times, was investigating a group of thirteen "Palmers" sold through a London dealer. Her second article, on 10 August, named Keating, and on 20 August he admitted the Palmer fakes and many others in a letter to the paper.1 His defence was that he had always planted clues: deliberate mistakes, or modern paint. Other forgers went further. Frank Kelley signed his fake Impressionists in white lead, which shows up plainly in X-rays. In postwar Germany the restorer Lothar Malskat, hired to restore bomb-damaged medieval frescoes in a church, simply painted a "lost" medieval cycle; the government printed four million postage stamps of it.2 When he confessed, nobody believed him, until he pointed to a turkey (a bird unknown in medieval Europe) and a portrait of the film star Marlene Dietrich in his "medieval" paintings.

Keating was charged with conspiracy to defraud in 1977, but the case, due for trial in 1979, was dropped because his health had collapsed; he died in 1984. Meanwhile he became a celebrity, with a television series on the techniques of the old masters. In a final twist, his fakes began to sell as Keatings for up to ten thousand pounds each, and other artists began forging Keatings.

concepts.title: Beltracchi: Painting the Pictures That Were Lost
concepts.contentHtml:
For more than 30 years the German forger Wolfgang Beltracchi and his wife Helene ran a forgery business that fooled buyers and galleries around the world. Wolfgang did not copy existing paintings. He painted new ones in the styles of dead European artists such as Max Ernst, Fernand Léger, Kees van Dongen and André Derain, and often gave them the titles of works known from old records to be lost, of which no pictures existed. A newly "found" lost work fills a gap instead of raising a question.

The provenance was invented with equal care. The couple claimed the works came from Helene's grandfather, who had supposedly acquired them from a Jewish gallerist fleeing Hitler's Germany, a story that explained why nobody had seen them. They bought old frames and canvases at flea markets and used a 1920s camera to take old-looking photographs of the paintings as evidence of their history. The fakes fooled Sotheby's and Christie's, which put one on the cover of an evening sale catalogue; one entered the collection of the actor Steve Martin; and a historian mistakenly authenticated one as a Max Ernst.

One tube of paint brought it all down. Wolfgang ran out of the zinc white he used and bought a zinc pigment from a Dutch manufacturer that did not disclose it contained titanium.1 Red Picture with Horses, passed off as a 1914 work by the Expressionist Heinrich Campendonk, sold at auction for a record 2.8 million euros (then $3.6 million). Analysis found titanium, but titanium white was only used as a pigment from the 1920s. That single anachronism unravelled everything. In 2011 the couple were convicted over 14 works,2 sentenced to six and four years in prison and ordered to pay 35 million euros in damages; they claim to have made around 300 fakes, many never identified. As Charney notes, this is how most forgers fall: not to an expert's eye but to a material that could not have existed on the date the picture claims.

title: Looted: Nazi Plunder and the Long Road Home
description: How the Nazis stole Europe's art, how the Monuments Men tracked it, and why restitution is still unfinished

concepts.title: The Machinery of Plunder
concepts.contentHtml:
Some of the twentieth century's greatest art thefts were organised by a government. The Nazi regime seized art from Jewish families, from museums and from churches across occupied Europe, and its main instrument was the Einsatzstab Reichsleiter Rosenberg (ERR), a task force created by the Nazi ideologue Alfred Rosenberg to gather the finest artworks for the Führermuseum, the vast museum Hitler planned for Linz in Austria.

The looters were meticulous record-keepers.1 The ERR listed and photographed what it took in large leather-bound albums, which were later used as evidence at the Nuremberg trials to convict Nazi criminals. In 1947 the US military handed 39 albums to the US National Archives, although more than 100 are thought to have been made. In occupied Paris, the artistic heritage of France passed through the small Jeu de Paume museum, and Hermann Göring made frequent shopping trips there, picking looted art for Hitler's Linz museum and for his own vast personal collection.

One woman watched it all. Rose Valland, who worked at the Jeu de Paume, eavesdropped on German conversations and secretly kept meticulous notes on where each train shipment was going.2 Had the Nazis discovered how much she knew, they would surely have killed her. After the war her paper trail led investigators to an enormous cache of looted art at Neuschwanstein Castle in Bavaria, and on to other hiding places. Even the most stolen artwork in history was caught up. The Ghent Altarpiece, sent away by Belgium for safekeeping, was moved on Hitler's orders to Neuschwanstein, an ERR depot, in August 1942, and was later hidden in an Austrian salt mine.

concepts.title: The Monuments Men (and Women)
concepts.contentHtml:
The Allies answered with an unusual unit. In June 1943 the United States set up a commission to protect Europe's art and monuments, eventually known as the Roberts Commission, and from it grew the Monuments, Fine Arts, and Archives section (MFAA): about 345 men and women from 14 nations.1 Their first job was to keep Allied troops from needlessly destroying cultural sites and to patch up damaged monuments; as the scale of the looting became clear, they ended up responsible for recovering and returning millions of objects. The nickname, the Monuments Men, hides the fact that women served too, among them the American officers Edith Standen, Evelyn Tucker and Mary Regan.

Their most famous find began with a toothache. Major Robert Posey, an architect, was sent to a local dentist whose son-in-law turned out to be an art scholar who had worked for Göring and Rosenberg. His information led in May 1945 to a salt mine at Altaussee in Austria, one of the largest repositories of stolen art. Local miners had blocked the entrances after realising that Nazi soldiers meant to destroy everything inside.2 In the mine lay Michelangelo's sculpture the Bruges Madonna, Vermeer's The Astronomer and the Ghent Altarpiece. The conservator George Stout organised their removal to a collecting point in Munich, where objects were identified and sent home. By 1951, more than five million items had been returned to their countries of origin.

The officers also watched their own side. Their files record looting by American soldiers. And on 7 November 1945, 24 of them signed the Wiesbaden Manifesto, protesting a US decision to ship 202 paintings from German collections,3 by artists from Botticelli to Vermeer, to the National Gallery of Art in Washington. They warned it would align the United States with the Nazis, who had used the same pretext of protection to justify their looting. One organiser later called it the only act of protest by officers against their orders in the Second World War. The paintings went anyway, but after an exhibition and a tour of 13 American cities they returned to Germany.

concepts.title: The Woman in Gold Goes Home
concepts.contentHtml:
Returning loot proved slower than finding it. Consider Gustav Klimt's Portrait of Adele Bloch-Bauer I (1907), the "Woman in Gold": an enormous, shimmering portrait in gold and oil on canvas of the wife of a Viennese Jewish sugar magnate, Ferdinand Bloch-Bauer. Critics called her "an idol in a golden shrine". Today it hangs in the Neue Galerie in New York.

Adele died in 1925, aged 43. Her will asked her husband to give their Klimts to the Austrian state gallery when he died, but it was a request, not a binding gift,1 and the paintings were his, because he had paid for them. In 1938, as Hitler annexed Austria, Ferdinand fled; his property was plundered by top Nazis and the Klimts were seized. Strangest of all, the portrait reached Vienna's national gallery through a Nazi lawyer with a letter signed "Heil Hitler",2 and the Nazis called it "The Dame in Gold" rather than reveal that it portrayed a woman from a prominent Jewish family. After the war, Austria claimed that Adele had willed the paintings to the gallery. Ferdinand died in Switzerland, leaving his property to his nephews and nieces. Only in 1998 did investigative articles in the Austrian press reveal the true story.

That year two rules changed. Austria passed a law requiring its museums to return art seized by the Nazis, and in December an international conference agreed the Washington Principles: non-binding guidelines that looted art should be identified, archives opened and a "just and fair solution" found. Ferdinand's niece Maria Altmann, with the lawyer E. Randol Schoenberg, took Austria to the US Supreme Court, which ruled in 2004 that she could sue. Austria agreed to arbitration, and in January 2006 the arbitrators ruled that five Klimts must be returned. Ronald Lauder then bought Adele for $135 million, a record at the time, for his museum. Was it fair? Altmann had once offered to let Austria keep the portrait if it admitted the painting was stolen, and it refused. The Principles themselves accept that solutions vary with the facts of each case,3 which is why many claims remain unresolved.

title: Who Says It's Real?
description: Experts, dealers and doubt: the Knoedler fakes, the $450 million Salvator Mundi and the Getty kouros

concepts.title: The Knoedler Affair
concepts.contentHtml:
A forger needs someone respectable to vouch for the work, and few vouchers were grander than Knoedler & Co. The gallery opened in New York in 1846, almost a quarter of a century before the Metropolitan Museum of Art was founded,1 and sold Old Masters to Cornelius Vanderbilt, J. P. Morgan and Henry Clay Frick. In 1994, the year Ann Freedman became its director, a Long Island dealer nobody had heard of, Glafira Rosales, began bringing her unknown works by Abstract Expressionists such as Mark Rothko, Jackson Pollock and Robert Motherwell. They came, she said, from an anonymous collector, known around the gallery as "Mr. X".

Every one was a fake, painted by Pei-Shen Qian, a Chinese immigrant artist, in his studio in Woodhaven, Queens. Between 1994 and 2008 dozens of counterfeits passed through Knoedler, and estimates of the total run from $60 million to $80 million. In 2004 the collectors Domenico and Eleanore De Sole paid $8.3 million for a "Rothko", reassured by a letter listing eleven experts said to have viewed it. Warning signs were everywhere: no receipts, sales records or photographs, a provenance story that kept shifting (at one point it involved a secret love affair) and huge profit margins. The forensic analyst James Martin found pigments in some of the works that were not invented until long after their supposed dates. And a "Pollock" with the signature misspelled "Pollok" hung in Freedman's own apartment for 15 years.2

Knoedler closed abruptly in November 2011. In 2013 Rosales pleaded guilty to wire fraud, money laundering and tax evasion; Qian returned to China, saying he never knew his paintings were being passed off as originals. Freedman has always said she relied on experts and was deceived too, pointing out that she bought several of the works herself; buyers argued that the red flags were obvious. The De Soles' case settled in 2016, just before Freedman was due to testify. The affair left a chill: as the Egon Schiele expert Jane Kallir notes, fear of costly litigation has caused many experts to stop issuing opinions of authenticity at all.3

concepts.title: The $450 Million Question
concepts.contentHtml:
Attribution, deciding who made a work, is the art historian's central judgement, and no case shows its stakes better than Salvator Mundi ("Saviour of the World"). It shows Christ raising his right hand in blessing and holding a crystal orb in his left, painted on a walnut panel1 that was once broken into two parts. In 1958 it sold at Sotheby's in London for £45 as a work by Leonardo's assistant Boltraffio.2 In 2005 a group of dealers bought it from an estate in New Orleans for $1,000 plus $175 commission.3 It was heavily damaged and overpainted, and the restorers Mario and Dianne Modestini repainted much of it.

Then its fortunes soared. In 2011 the National Gallery in London showed it as one of nine paintings by Leonardo in a major exhibition. In 2013 it sold privately for $75–80 million and was swiftly resold for $127.5 million. In November 2017 it sold at Christie's in New York for $450.3 million, making it the world's most expensive work of art, to a buyer acting for Saudi Arabia's crown prince, Mohammed bin Salman. Then it vanished from view: it never went on show at the Louvre Abu Dhabi as announced, and it was missing from the Louvre's great Leonardo exhibition in 2019.

Scholars still disagree, and the evidence cuts both ways:

  • An unpublished Louvre study, using X-rays and infrared images, concluded the painting is by Leonardo, citing a very fine underdrawing like that of the Mona Lisa and changes of mind (pentimenti) such as a moved thumb.
  • A 2021 documentary quoted French officials who said the Louvre's laboratory found Leonardo "only contributed" to it.
  • The Leonardo specialist Carmen Bambach describes it as a work by Boltraffio painted under Leonardo's close supervision around 1505–10.

When it sold, the Metropolitan Museum's then chief executive, Thomas Campbell, posted a pre-restoration photograph with the words "#readthesmallprint". Money, politics and repaint now press on a question that is, in the end, one of judgement.

concepts.title: Greek, About 530 B.C., or Modern Forgery
concepts.contentHtml:
The J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles owns a statue with perhaps the most honest label in the art world. The Getty kouros is a marble statue of a standing nude youth just over two metres tall (206.1 centimetres). Like other kouroi of Archaic Greece, he stands with his left foot forward, arms at his sides, looking straight ahead; he was carved in from four sides so that he keeps the shape of the original block, and his muscles are reduced to decorative patterns on the surface. Such statues served as dedications to the gods or as grave monuments, and stood for the idea of youth rather than any one young man.

The Getty bought it in 1985 from a dealer in Basel, Switzerland. Its date is given as "about 530 B.C. or modern forgery". Why the doubt? The statue mixes earlier and later stylistic traits, and it is carved from marble from the island of Thasos at a date when that marble is unexpected.1 Scientists published studies of the weathering of its dolomitic marble, and in 1990 the scholar Jeffery Spier discussed it in an article pointedly titled "Blinded by Science: The Abuse of Science in the Detection of False Antiquities". In 1992 the statue was exhibited in Athens and specialists debated it at a colloquium there. Neither art historians nor scientists have settled the question.2

The Getty's own text makes a point worth remembering: the oddities "may be due more to our limited knowledge of Greek sculpture in this period rather than to mistakes on the part of a forger." A fake is spotted by comparing it with genuine works, so when the genuine record is thin, the unusual and the forged can look alike. The kouros is a lesson in intellectual honesty: sometimes the right answer is "we do not know", and a good museum says so on its label.

title: The Lab Strikes Back
description: Pigments, tree rings, the bomb pulse and AI: what science can prove about a painting, and what it cannot

concepts.title: Reading a Painting in Layers
concepts.contentHtml:
A conservator thinks of a painting as a stack of four layers: the support (usually wood or canvas), the ground that prepares it, the paint, and the varnish on top. Each layer can hold evidence, and modern tools read many of them without harming the picture:

  • X-radiography passes through most paint but is stopped by lead white and by vermilion, a mercury red, so it reveals changes made in those pigments and the construction of the support, including saw marks. Regular marks from a mechanical saw on a supposedly seventeenth-century panel are a strong sign of a fake.1
  • Infrared reflectography sees through paint to any drawing beneath. An artist inventing a picture may sketch first; a copyist has little need to.
  • Ultraviolet light makes later repainting show up as dark spots and tells varnishes apart: shellac fluoresces orange.
  • X-ray fluorescence identifies the chemical elements in a pigment without taking a sample.

The most decisive clue is a material anachronism, a substance that did not exist when the work was supposedly made. Cadmium yellow was introduced about 1800, so when it turned up in a still life that the St Louis Art Museum bought in 1942 as a work by Francisco de Zurbarán (1598–1664), the attribution collapsed.2 Acrylic paints first became available in the 1930s, and titanium white came into use in the 1920s, as Beltracchi discovered. But a pigment only gives a terminus post quem, an earliest possible date, and old pigments can be revived: lead-tin yellow disappeared around 1850 and was rediscovered in 1941. Age also shows in craquelure, the network of cracks in old paint, whose extent should match the claimed date; some forgers have simply painted lines on to imitate it.

Science can rescue a painting too. A small Virgin and Child first attributed to Jan Gossaert had been consigned to the storerooms of the National Gallery in London as a later copy. Tests in 1994 found nineteenth-century repainting over older layers containing a sixteenth-century red, on a support of matching age. Once the later paint was removed, the original Gossaert reappeared.3

concepts.title: Clocks in Wood, Clay, Canvas and Oil
concepts.contentHtml:
Some materials carry their own clocks. Oak panels can be dated by dendrochronology, because the pattern of rings in the wood records the years in which the tree was alive. The same logic exposes fake instruments: a violin with a spruce soundboard from a tree felled after 1890 cannot be a Stradivarius, since the last ones were made in the early eighteenth century.1 For pottery there is thermoluminescence: minerals in fired clay slowly store energy, and when heated they release it as light whose intensity reflects the time since the object was last fired. Glazing, construction techniques and thermoluminescence together exposed the Metropolitan Museum's monumental "Etruscan" terracotta warriors, displayed in New York for three decades, as modern.

Canvas, paper and the oil in paint all come from plants, so they can be dated by radiocarbon (the nuclear chemistry topic explains the decay clock). The catch is that dating a canvas tells you when its fibres were harvested, not when the picture was painted, and forgers know it: van Meegeren scraped old paintings to reuse their canvases, and Beltracchi bought old supports at flea markets.

The answer is to date the paint itself, using an odd gift of the Cold War. Nuclear weapons tests between 1954 and 1963 sharply raised the carbon-14 in the atmosphere, and it has declined ever since; anything that grew in those decades carries this bomb pulse. In a 2019 study, researchers tested a folk-style painting signed "Sarah Honn May 5, 1866 AD", a known fake by the forger Robert Trotter, who admitted 52 sales of fakes between 1981 and 1988.2 The canvas gave a broad date range that did not contradict 1866. But a paint chip weighing 160 micrograms, which left just 19 micrograms of carbon after cleaning, showed the bomb-pulse excess: the seeds that gave the oil were harvested in 1958–61 or 1983–89.3 Trotter had confessed to painting it in 1985. The method has limits. Varnish, repairs and conservation materials add carbon of other ages, and most real paintings are harder to sample than this one.

concepts.title: Can a Machine Tell Rubens from a Copy?
concepts.contentHtml:
The newest tool is artificial intelligence. Researchers train neural networks on photographs of an artist's accepted works and of imitations, then ask the network to judge a new image, often patch by patch. In a 2023 study, a vision transformer trained on authentic van Gogh paintings and a set of imitations told them apart with an accuracy of over 85%.1 Because so few known forgeries exist to learn from, another team added fakes generated by the image models Stable Diffusion and StyleGAN to the training data, and found that the synthetic forgeries consistently improved the detection of human-made ones.

Real cases are messier. In 2025 the Zurich company Art Recognition analysed a version of Rubens's The Bath of Diana (around 1635) that had long been thought a copy. Its AI examined 29 patches: ten came out as clearly authentic, with probabilities over 80%,2 while the figure of Diana herself scored as not by Rubens's hand, suggesting a work partly by Rubens and partly by his studio. The company's chief executive, Carina Popovici, called it "an authenticity evaluation not a confirmation". Nils Büttner, chairman of the Centrum Rubenianum, which compiles the catalogue of Rubens's works, replied that a condition report shows it "is not the real thing".

Sceptics point to built-in limits. An AI sees only digital photographs, whose quality depends on the camera and the lighting; training can need thousands of images, and few artists made that many works. It cannot weigh documents, materials or the feel of a support. Jane Kallir argues that forensic testing "may rule out an attribution, but it is not sufficient to make one3", and AI is no different. That is the lesson of this whole topic, and of the forged manuscripts in Sacred Forgeries: the strongest verdicts combine the paper trail, the expert eye and the laboratory. A fake has to fool all three; the truth only has to survive them.
